A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
beneficiary
A person who receives an advantage or payment.
consolidate
To combine separate items into one reported figure.
qualify
To limit or make a statement more precise.
authorisation
Official approval for an action or payment.
misstate
To give a fact or figure incorrectly.
disclose
To make information available to others.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The annual accounts had the reassuring appearance of precision: totals arranged in columns, notes beneath them, a statement of expenditure that invited the reader to believe every pound had been accounted for. Emma knew better than to mistake financial presentation for a transaction history. The figure for student assistance was an aggregate. It could establish what the Glenarraidh Education Trust reported spending; it could not, by itself, identify beneficiaries, authorising officers or the purpose of individual transfers.

Sarah rang as Emma compared the report with her notes from the withheld call.

“Doesn't the lack of names tell us something?”

“It tells us the report doesn't contain names,” Emma replied. “Whether the underlying records are absent is another question.”

They created three headings: Reported, Alleged and Unverified. Emma placed the caller's instruction in the second category, not the first. Whoever had telephoned might possess inside knowledge, but neither his authority nor his motive had been established.

Fiona Bell's reply arrived before midday. She confirmed that the trust's board had met in September 2011, qualifying the impression left by the incomplete online index. Some historical minutes had been transferred to storage, she wrote, although she had not personally examined the relevant boxes. She would ask the records team to establish whether copies could be located and whether any could be made available for inspection.

As for the accounts, Fiona explained that the published line for educational assistance consolidated multiple grants. It was not intended as a beneficiary-by-beneficiary schedule. Emma noted what Fiona had confirmed and, equally carefully, what she had not: nothing about the authenticity of a particular payment, the existence of a signed authorisation or any deliberate concealment.

Later, at the library, Emma consulted the paper edition of a local newspaper whose early archives were incomplete online. A photograph from a 2011 fundraising evening showed Claire with several prospective students; Malcolm Vale stood at the far side of the group. Beneath it, the caption repeated the trust's pledge to support travel expenses for courses beyond Glenarraidh.

She captured the complete page, including publication date, rather than cropping away its context. A public pledge was relevant to Claire's concerns about promises and outcomes. It was not evidence that any named student had been deprived of support.

The more intriguing discovery appeared almost by accident: a small correction in a subsequent issue. The paper acknowledged that its earlier coverage had misstated the number of students involved in the travel programme. The correction did not supply the revised figure or explain the source of the original mistake.

For several seconds Emma imagined the discrepancy as the first visible crack in an elaborate deception. Then she stopped. A numerical error could arise in reporting, administration or communication without indicating fraud. The proper next step was to retrieve the initial article, establish precisely what had been claimed and compare it with whatever grant schedules the trust might lawfully disclose.

Sarah texted to ask whether the accounts had yielded anything substantial.

Not yet, Emma wrote. We have a public promise, a summary figure and an unresolved correction. No evidence of an improper transfer.

She set the two newspaper references beside Fiona's email. The anonymous voice had attempted to supply a conclusion and a route towards it. Emma would follow the documentary trail instead.

As she closed her notebook, she noticed something else about the correction: it referred not merely to the number of applicants, but specifically to the number of students selected. That distinction had appeared nowhere in the public statement she had just read. She circled the word and wrote one question underneath.

Selected by whom?
